title: A better invoice check starts with three records.
description: Bring the agreement, delivery record and invoice into one review, so every difference has context and a clear next step.
alt: Three cream paper records joined by a violet cord, illustrating a connected invoice review.
intro: An invoice tells you what a supplier has charged. It cannot, by itself, tell you whether that charge matches the agreement or what arrived. A useful review brings those records together before anyone decides that a line is wrong.
takeaway: Keep the agreement, delivery evidence and invoice line together. A difference is a question to investigate, not a conclusion.

sections.title: Start with the right version of each record.
paragraphs: Choose one invoice and identify the agreement that applied to that purchase. It might be an accepted quote, a dated price list or a purchase order. A newer price list is not automatically the right reference for an earlier delivery. Keep the effective date and any agreed exceptions with the document.

Then find the receiving record: the delivery note, goods-received entry or other evidence your team uses to record what arrived. A supplier’s dispatch note and your team’s receiving record may describe different events. Keep both when that distinction matters.

Finally, connect the invoice to those records using the supplier, site, order reference and delivery date. Similar product names are not enough to establish a match. If the connection is uncertain, record that uncertainty instead of forcing a comparison.

sections.title: Compare a line, not just the total.
paragraphs: Work through product, quantity, unit and price in that order. Confirm that a case on the invoice means the same case size as the agreement. Check whether a weight refers to an individual item or the whole delivery. Only then compare the figures.

In Margevia’s fictional Greenfield example, the agreed chicken price is €8.40 per kg and the invoice shows €9.10 per kg for 120 kg. The difference is €84 on that line. A separate olive-oil difference adds €12, bringing the sample invoice’s flagged amount to €96. These are amounts to review, not credits received.

rows: What product, unit and price were agreed?
What product, quantity and price were billed?

sections.title: Write down what needs resolving.
paragraphs: A useful exception note is specific: invoice reference, line item, expected figure, invoiced figure, difference and links to the supporting records. Add the name of the person who will investigate and the next action. This gives a colleague enough context to continue without rebuilding the review.

Avoid turning an uncertain match into an accusation. A pack-size change, replacement product or documented price revision may explain the difference. If the evidence supports the charge, close the exception with that explanation so it does not keep returning to the queue.

sections.title: Make the first review easy to repeat.
paragraphs: Start with a small set of invoices from one site and a few suppliers. Notice where the work slows down: finding the agreement, understanding a unit, locating a receiving note or deciding who should follow up. Those observations are more useful than a large pile of unexplained flags.

A repeatable review leaves two things behind: a clear reason for every exception and a clear next step for every unresolved one. Margevia’s preview lets you explore that approach with fictional records before considering how it might fit your team.

title: Two pack sizes. One fair comparison.
shortTitle: Compare the unit before the price
description: A different pack price is not always a price increase. Check product, pack size and quantity before flagging a discrepancy.
alt: Two boxes hold six small containers and three larger containers, with a violet measuring bar below.
intro: One supplier quotes by the case. Another invoices by the bottle. A replacement comes in a different size. The figures can look inconsistent even when the underlying unit price is the same. Put the units on the same footing before deciding what changed.
takeaway: Normalize quantities only after confirming that the product, specification and applicable terms are comparable.

sections.title: Make sure it is the same purchase.
paragraphs: Start with the product reference and specification. Similar descriptions can hide a different grade, concentration, preparation or brand. A substitute may have been accepted by the kitchen even though the invoice line still resembles the original order.

Keep the supplier’s item reference next to your internal name. If a replacement was agreed, link the approval rather than silently treating the two items as identical. You want a reviewer to see why a comparison is valid, not just the result of a calculation.

sections.title: Use a common unit you can explain.
paragraphs: For a liquid, litres may be a useful common unit. For a weighed ingredient, kilograms may be appropriate. For individually counted products, use a consistent count. The choice depends on what was purchased and how the agreement describes it.

Consider this illustrative example: a case of six one-litre bottles costs €60. A case of twelve half-litre bottles also costs €60. Both contain six litres, so both work out at €10 per litre. Comparing only the bottle price would make the second case appear cheaper, even though the price per litre is unchanged.

sections.title: Keep the surrounding terms visible.
paragraphs: A unit conversion does not settle every question. Check whether the figures include the same charges, discounts and other price components. Avoid comparing a base product price with a figure that includes an extra delivery charge, or an earlier quote with a later approved revision.

Where an invoice bundles a charge that the agreement lists separately, preserve the original presentation and explain your comparison. Do not overwrite the source values with normalized ones. A colleague should be able to trace the result back to the record without reverse-engineering your spreadsheet.

sections.title: Make an uncertain conversion visible.
paragraphs: If a pack size is missing, the useful next action is to confirm it. Guessing can create a convincing but false exception. Label the missing detail and identify who can resolve it: the buyer, receiving team or supplier.

A small review note can hold the original unit, the common unit, the conversion used and its source. Once confirmed, that note can help the next reviewer recognize the same product. Recheck it when packaging or specifications change.

Margevia’s preview uses simple, clearly labeled quantities. Real records will be messier. Keeping the conversion visible is one way to make that complexity reviewable rather than hiding it behind a single difference amount.

title: When the invoice and delivery disagree.
description: Connect a billed quantity to receiving evidence, account for split deliveries and leave a clear record for supplier follow-up.
alt: A navy six-compartment delivery crate contains five ivory packages; a violet outline marks the empty compartment.
intro: An invoice can show the ordered quantity even when the delivery arrived in parts. It can also include an item that was refused, substituted or recorded elsewhere. Before raising a query, establish what happened at the receiving point.
takeaway: Separate ordered, dispatched, received and accepted quantities. They can describe different stages of the same purchase.

sections.title: Find the delivery behind the charge.
paragraphs: Match the invoice to the site, order and delivery references. A supplier may combine several deliveries on one invoice, while a site may receive a single order over several days. Reviewing only one delivery note can make a correct charge look too high.

Bring the receiving evidence into the review. That could include a recorded count, a note about a refused item or an agreed replacement. Keep the original date and reference visible. If the record is incomplete, say what is missing rather than inferring a shortage from the absence of paperwork.

sections.title: Distinguish what was ordered from what arrived.
paragraphs: Ordered quantity describes the request. Dispatched quantity describes what the supplier says it sent. Received quantity describes what reached the site. Accepted quantity may differ again when goods were refused or returned. Use the distinctions your own receiving process can support.

In Margevia’s fictional Harbour Fresh example, an invoice bills 30 units at €7 each while the sample delivery reference shows 24. The six-unit difference produces €42 to investigate. The example assumes the units match and there is no second delivery or other adjustment explaining the charge.

callout.label: Illustrative calculation
callout.text: 30 billed − 24 received = 6 units to check. At €7 per unit, the flagged difference is €42.

sections.title: Give the supplier a question they can answer.
paragraphs: State the invoice number, relevant line, billed quantity and receiving reference. Explain the mismatch and ask for the record or adjustment that resolves it. A concise, evidence-backed question is easier to work with than a general statement that the invoice is wrong.

Keep substitutions, returns and later deliveries attached to the same review. When new evidence arrives, update the case instead of opening an unrelated note. The goal is a single account of what happened, even if several people contribute to it.

sections.title: Close the issue with evidence.
paragraphs: A supplier reply may explain the charge, confirm a corrected invoice or promise a credit. Record which outcome actually occurred. A promise of an adjustment and a received adjustment are different states; do not collapse them into one completed checkbox.

For unresolved cases, keep an owner and the next follow-up date visible. For resolved cases, link the explanation or correcting document. This makes the handoff between operations, purchasing and finance easier to follow.

The Margevia preview demonstrates the difference and the review action with fictional records. It does not contact suppliers or confirm real credits. Its purpose is to make the proposed review path clear enough for teams to discuss.

title: Flagged is not recovered: follow the credit through.
description: Keep evidence, supplier responses and confirmed adjustments connected without counting every flagged amount as a saving.
alt: A violet thread links three folded paper records on a navy surface; the final record has a muted green tab.
intro: Finding a discrepancy creates work to do. It does not establish that the supplier agrees, that an adjustment is due or that money has been recovered. A useful follow-up process preserves those distinctions all the way to resolution.
takeaway: Track the amount flagged, the amount supported by review and the adjustment actually confirmed as separate facts.

sections.title: Give each state a concrete meaning.
paragraphs: Start with language that tells the next person what has happened. “Needs review” means a difference has been identified. “Ready for follow-up” means someone has checked the evidence and prepared a question. “Awaiting response” means the question has actually been sent.

After the supplier responds, record the outcome: explained charge, disputed difference, promised adjustment or received correcting document. Choose the labels that fit your process, but define them clearly enough that two colleagues would classify the same case in the same way.

sections.title: Keep the amount attached to its explanation.
paragraphs: An amount without context is difficult to act on. Keep the supplier, invoice reference, site, line item and reason for the query together. Link the agreement or receiving evidence that supports it. Record partial adjustments without losing the original amount under discussion.

Suppose a fictional review flags €96, but a documented price revision explains €12. The amount still requiring follow-up is then €84. If a later credit covers only €60, the remaining €24 needs its own outcome. The stages tell the story more accurately than one headline total.

callout.label: Keep the stages separate
callout.text: €96 initially flagged → €84 still supported after review → €60 credited → €24 awaiting an outcome. Illustrative figures only.

sections.title: Assign the next action, not just the case.
paragraphs: A name in an owner column is useful only when the next action is clear. The buyer may need to confirm an agreement, the receiving team may need to locate a note, or finance may need to verify a credit document. Record that specific step and when it should be revisited.

If someone hands the case over, keep the previous exchange with it. Repeatedly asking for the same evidence creates more work for both sides and makes it harder to see whether the question has changed.

sections.title: Measure the completed outcome honestly.
paragraphs: When reviewing the process, separate cases explained without an adjustment, cases still open and cases with confirmed correcting documents. If you track monetary outcomes, use a definition your team has agreed and check the evidence behind it. Avoid presenting the whole exception queue as recovered money.

Margevia follows that distinction in its sample workspace. The review button prepares a local follow-up state; it does not send a supplier message or record a real credit. That boundary is intentional: the interface should make the decision clearer without claiming an outcome that has not happened.

title: Why we’re building Margevia around the review.
description: The thinking behind a product concept that keeps source evidence, human judgment and the next action in the same picture.
alt: A violet bridge connects two stacks of cream paper beside a graphite pencil, representing the Margevia product idea.
intro: Margevia begins with a small question: does this invoice match what was agreed and delivered? We are building a product concept around making that question easier to answer, and making the next action easier to follow.
takeaway: The product should help someone understand a difference and decide what to do. The evidence matters as much as the flag.

sections.title: Start with a decision someone has to make.
paragraphs: A price list describes an agreement. A receiving note describes a delivery. An invoice asks for payment. Each record can be clear on its own, while the relationship between them still takes effort to reconstruct. That relationship is the starting point for Margevia.

The concept is designed for purchasing, operations and finance teams at small restaurant groups and independent caterers. We are not treating every team as if it has the same process. The person who knows whether a replacement was accepted may be different from the person checking the invoice, and a useful tool needs to respect that handoff.

sections.title: Put the evidence beside the conclusion.
paragraphs: A discrepancy flag should invite inspection. It should show which figures were compared, where they came from and what assumption connects them. If the units do not match, the applicable price is uncertain or a delivery record is missing, that uncertainty should stay visible.

This principle affects even a small interface decision. In the preview, the invoice line sits beside the reference figure, and the supporting record is named below. The amount is labeled for review. A reviewer can see the question before deciding whether it deserves a supplier conversation.

callout.label: A product principle
callout.text: Make the source of a difference visible before asking someone to act on it.

sections.title: Make the idea tangible before making promises.
paragraphs: The first public version is a lightweight interactive preview. It has three fictional invoices: a price-difference example, a delivery-difference example and a matched invoice. Visitors can move between them, inspect the numbers and try a local review action.

That is deliberately narrower than a production service. The preview does not process uploaded invoices, connect to accounting tools, send supplier messages or recover money. It gives the product conversation something concrete to refer to without presenting unbuilt capabilities as available.

sections.title: Let the workflow shape the next build.
paragraphs: The next useful questions are about the work itself. Where does a team keep the current agreement? Which delivery details are reliable? Who decides that a difference is valid? What evidence is needed before a case can be closed? Those answers should shape what gets built next.

We also want to learn where an extra tool would create friction. A clearer comparison is not enough if someone must duplicate records or maintain another disconnected list. A focused pilot would need to examine the whole handoff, including the work that remains manual.

This journal will share the thinking behind that process alongside practical review guides. Margevia is still a concept in development. The purpose of the preview is to make the idea understandable, invite specific feedback and give the next iteration a better foundation.

title: Three invoices, one idea: inside our first preview.
description: Why the first Margevia demo uses three fictional invoices, reversible review states and visible source evidence.
alt: Three ivory sample interface panels with violet markers stand on a lilac surface beside a navy pointer.
intro: A product idea is easier to discuss when people can try a small part of it. Our first preview focuses on one sequence: choose an invoice, understand a difference and decide whether it is ready for follow-up.
takeaway: A small, honest preview can test whether a workflow makes sense before live processing and integrations are built.

sections.title: Use three cases that ask different questions.
paragraphs: Greenfield Foods is the price-check case. Its fictional invoice totals €1,588.80 against a matched amount of €1,492.80, leaving €96 to review. The detail separates the €84 chicken-price difference from the €12 olive-oil difference so visitors can inspect the individual lines.

Harbour Fresh is the delivery case: €354 invoiced, €312 matched and €42 to investigate. Daily Provisions is the matched case: €228 on both sides and no difference. Including a matched record matters because a review interface should also explain when there is nothing to pursue.

sections.title: Let people explore without creating a real case.
paragraphs: The sample review action changes the record to “Ready for follow-up.” It can be reset, and it stays local to the current page visit. The matched invoice disables that action because there is no sample difference to prepare.

The comparison export contains fictional records and describes the review state. Neither the export nor the button sends a message to a supplier. Keeping that boundary explicit lets someone explore the workflow without confusing a demonstration with an operational action.

sections.title: Look for understanding before feature requests.
paragraphs: A useful walkthrough asks the visitor to explain what they see. Which amount would they investigate? Where would they look for the agreement? What would they need to confirm before sending a query? Can they tell the difference between a flagged amount and a received credit?

Those questions test the clarity of the proposed workflow. They also reveal missing context that a polished screen can conceal: a product substitution, an uncertain unit, a partial delivery or an approval that lives in an email. A future version should make those situations manageable rather than assume them away.

sections.title: Keep the stage of the product visible.
paragraphs: The preview is not an OCR service, an accounting integration or a live supplier-credit system. A 15-second motion film now illustrates the sample workflow in the Demo video tab. The pilot planner lets visitors choose a team, review focus and number of locations, while brief delivery remains unavailable until it is connected.

These boundaries tell us where the next work begins. Before processing real documents, we would need to define the review process, access, handling of records and responsibility for exceptions with a participating team. None of that is established by a sample dashboard alone.

For now, the preview offers a concrete way to discuss the idea. Try all three invoices and notice where you would need more information. The most useful feedback is a specific moment in the workflow that is unclear, missing or difficult to fit into the way your team already works.
